activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
story:
The warehouse smelled like cardboard and cold metal, and Owen stood in the doorway holding a rake he had carried over from the neighborhood cleanup in the park next door. He had signed up for the cleanup first, but when Ms. Popescu came by with a clipboard and asked for two more volunteers inside, he and Tobin had raised their hands at the same time. Now they stood in a huge room with shelves stacked to the ceiling, and there was not a single customer anywhere.

"Where are all the people getting their food?" Owen asked. He had anticipated a line at the door, maybe families with bags, the way the grocery store looked before a storm.

Tobin shrugged and hefted a crate of canned beans onto a dolly. "Ms. Popescu said to sort the donations onto these pallets. Maybe the people come later?"

Owen rolled his empty dolly down an aisle, past a rack of cereal, past a tower of pasta. The motion sensor above the loading dock door chirped and the door ratcheted upward as he passed, letting in a slab of afternoon light. On the wall near the office hung a whiteboard with a number on it: 1,842. Underneath, in smaller letters, "cumulative boxes sorted this year." He stared at it, then looked back down the endless aisles. This place was not built for handing out groceries. It was built for storing them, mountains of them, from all over the city.

He found Ms. Popescu taping labels onto pallets. "So if people don't come here," he said, "where do they go?"

"Somewhere closer to home," she said. "It's a food bank, not a food pantry." She pointed her tape dispenser at the shelves. "This is the warehouse. The pantries are the little places in the neighborhoods where folks pick up the food directly. We send it out to them."

"So that's why there's so much," Owen said. "One pantry couldn't hold all this." It was like the storm drain by his house, he thought, collecting from every gutter on the street.

He went back and worked the beans aisle with Tobin, racing him pallet to pallet, and by the time the light through the dock door had gone orange, they had added forty-one boxes to the cumulative count. Tobin wrote the new number in green marker, 1,883, and stood back to admire it.

Ms. Popescu came over with two bottles of water. "You two can ride along Thursday," she said. "The van delivers to the pantry on Birch Street in the morning."

Owen twisted the cap off his bottle and grinned. "I want to see the other end of it."

"Then be here at eight," she said, and slapped the side of the van twice, like it could hear him.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force.
story:
Raphael had been staring at the old photograph on his grandfather's wall for ten minutes before he finally said, "Grandpa, I don't get it. How did Germany build a huge army again only twenty years after losing the first war?"

His grandfather looked up from his crossword. "That's quite a question for a Sunday."

"I have to explain it tomorrow. In Mr. Bighorn's class. It's like an audition, only for your brain. If you do well, you get to be the one who presents at the assembly." Raphael pulled out his notebook, which was blank except for the words TREATY OF VERSAILLES underlined three times. "I know the treaty punished Germany. Mr. Bighorn said the treaty limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force. That's it. That's all I've got, and it doesn't answer anything. An army of 100,000 isn't big, so where did all the soldiers come from later?"

His grandfather set down his pencil and tapped the photograph. "Come here. You see this? That's my father, your great-grandfather, at the memorial in town. I was about your age when he took me there."

Raphael remembered that day, though it had been years ago. He had been eight, and he had asked his great-grandfather why the stone had so many names carved into it. His great-grandfather had said, "Because a war this size takes a whole country's worth of men," and Raphael had imagined an entire country marching in rows, on and on past the church, past the bakery, past the school, until the marchers blurred together like rain on a window.

"Grandpa," Raphael said slowly, "when the treaty cut the army down to 100,000, that's like taking a river and pinching it to a stream. The water doesn't disappear."

His grandfather raised an eyebrow. "Go on."

"The soldiers were still out there. Millions of them had gone home after the war. The treaty said the army could only have 100,000 soldiers, but it couldn't make the men who had already fought forget how to fight." Raphael started writing so fast his pen squeaked. "And the air force ban. It's the same trick. They banned the planes, but not the pilots, and not the people who knew how to build planes."

"That sounds like reasoning to me," his grandfather said. "But can you distinguish between what the treaty said on paper and what actually happened? Because a treaty is only paper."

"Exactly, that's the point!" Raphael was on his feet now, pacing between the armchair and the window. "The treaty said one thing, and the country did another. The rules looked strong, but there was all this... this fertile ground. All those trained men, all that knowledge, just waiting. And when things got bad enough, the rules on paper couldn't stop anything."

His phone buzzed. A message from Davina: "Did u figure out the army thing yet? Ulysse says it was magic. I told him he's wrong."

Raphael grinned and typed back, "Not magic. Tell Ulysse a rule is only as strong as whoever enforces it. Presentation is ON." Then he grabbed his notebook, kissed his grandfather on the cheek, and ran for the door, shouting over his shoulder, "I'll tell you how it went tomorrow!"

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The plain-folks technique presents a politician or company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as "one of us."
story:
The poster went up on Monday, right beside the water fountain: Marcus Delgado, candidate for student council president, photographed with a cafeteria tray, laughing with a table full of kids. Daniel studied it on his way to science. It said nothing about what Marcus planned to do. It only said, in thick letters, "JUST ONE OF US."

"His mom took that picture," Alma said, appearing beside him with her backpack half unzipped. "I was there. He bought everyone fries."

"Do you know his platform?" Daniel asked.

"His what?"

"His plan. For the school."

Alma shrugged. "He seems normal. That's basically the whole pitch."

Daniel was skeptical, mostly because Marcus had spent the previous year giving announcements in a fake British accent. He went to find Paris, who was taping up his own campaign poster in the east stairwell. Paris's poster was a spreadsheet, printed in grayscale, listing three proposals with costs estimated from the supply closet price list.

"Nobody's going to vote for a spreadsheet," Paris said, without looking up.

"Then don't let them vote for a guy holding a taco," Daniel said. "Ask him his plan. In front of everyone."

Tuesday was the assembly, and each candidate got two minutes. Marcus went first. He wore a hoodie, which Daniel noted was a different hoodie than the one in the poster, and he told a story about missing the bus and having to walk four miles, "because I know what regular students go through." The gym applauded. A kid near the bleachers shouted, "He's just like us!" which, Daniel reflected, might have been rehearsed, since it was Marcus's cousin.

When Paris got the microphone, he said only, "Marcus, what's your actual plan for the vending machines?" Daniel watched the moment land. Marcus smiled, rubbed the back of his neck, and said he'd been talking with a lot of students about that very thing. He named no plan. He named no students either.

In Mr. Ricci's fifth period, they were doing propaganda posters from history, and one showed a politician in overalls leaning on a fence. Mr. Ricci asked the class what they noticed. Nobody answered. Daniel raised his hand.

"Plain-folks," he said. "It's when somebody acts ordinary so you trust them. Like they're one of us."

Mr. Ricci pointed at him with the chalk. "Correct."

At lunch, Alma slid her tray next to Daniel's. "So you're saying the fries were a strategy."

"The fries were a strategy," Daniel said. "The hoodie was a strategy. The walking-four-miles story, I'd put money on it."

The election was Thursday. Paris won by eleven votes, which Alma called a miracle and Daniel called four hundred fries down the drain. In the hallway afterward, Marcus stopped at the water fountain beside his own poster. He looked at it for a long moment, then peeled off one corner with his thumbnail.

"Do me a favor," he said. "Next year, tell me sooner."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house.
story:
The lights died at 7:42, right in the middle of Eva's homework, and the whole apartment went black as a cave. From the kitchen she heard her grandmother's slippers shuffling toward the drawer where the candles lived.

"Wait, Grandma, no candles," Eva called, scrambling toward the sound of shuffling. "Flashlights, the drawer next to the stove. Mr. Das made us memorize it in fire safety last spring."

In the dark, her grandmother snorted. "Candles worked for a hundred years before your Mr. Das."

Eva's fingers found the flashlight and clicked it on. The beam caught her grandmother mid-reach, one hand hovering over a fat white candle, and Eva thought of the demonstration Mr. Das had done in class. He had held up a flashlight and said safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut, because a candle can easily start a fire in a dark house. Then he had waved the flashlight around like a sword and accidentally knocked a marker off the desk, which had somehow made everyone remember it better.

"See, that's why," Eva said, sweeping the beam in her own pretend-sword arc and clipping a cereal box off the counter. "Oops. Okay, maybe don't copy that part."

Her grandmother laughed and took the second flashlight, and for a while they sat in the living room eating crackers by twin beams, pretending they were camping. Down the hall, someone in 4B stomped three times, the building's signal for "is it just us?" Eva stomped back twice: "just the power, we're fine." She felt oddly competent, like someone who knew the secret rules of dark buildings.

Then came a knock. It was Austen from down the hall, holding a dripping birthday cake with one lone candle stuck in the top. "The power died before I could light it for my mom," he said mournfully. "You don't happen to have a match?"

Eva's grandmother raised her flashlight solemnly. "We have something better than a match, and better than a candle, for lighting your way. But for the cake itself, one careful candle, watched every second, at the table with nothing flammable near it."

"Candle supervision," Eva said. "My new job title."

They lit the single candle in the middle of Austen's kitchen table, and it glowed over the frosting while everyone sang in the dark. Right at "happy birthday dear Mom," all the lights blazed back on, brighter than ever, and the little candle sat there looking pointless in the glare.

"Perfect timing," Austen's mom said, and blew it out anyway.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A Presta valve has a small nut on top that must be unscrewed before any air can be pumped in or let out.
story:
The driving school shared its back lot with a bike repair club that met on Saturdays, which was why Victoria found herself kneeling on warm asphalt behind a strip mall, a punctured inner tube spread across her knees. Ms. Santos-Reyes had agreed to run the club as long as nobody rode across the orange cones she used for her student drivers, and the cones now orbited the lot in a wide lazy loop, marking imaginary turns.

"First lever goes under the bead," Alvin said, watching from a folding chair. He had done this twice already and acted like a mechanic, though he had snapped a lever the week before.

Victoria slid the flat end of the plastic lever under the edge of the tyre and pushed down. The rubber resisted, then popped over the rim like a lid coming off a jar. She worked the second lever around, and the whole side of the tyre loosened. Rocco, who was supposed to be pumping the spare tube as a test, was already red in the face.

"Nothing," he panted. "I'm pumping and it's like pumping a rock. The pump does nothing."

"Then it's a bad pump," Alvin said.

Victoria didn't answer. She looked at the tube in her hands, then at the pump hose in Rocco's, and a thought circled her like the cones circled the lot. If the pump was bad, it would feel loose or hiss. Rocco said it felt solid, like the air had nowhere to go. That wasn't a broken pump. That was a closed door somewhere. She held the valve of her spare tube up to the light. At the top sat a tiny brass nut, screwed snug against a little pin. Her thumb turned it counterclockwise, one full rotation, and she pushed the pin once with a fingernail. A whisper of air escaped.

"It's called a Presta valve," she said. "There's a small nut on top. It has to be unscrewed before any air can go in or come out."

Rocco looked at his tube, found the same little nut, and unscrewed it. His next pump stroke sank smooth and easy, and the tube fattened under his hands. "So every time it goes flat and every time we fill it?"

"That's the rule, I think," Victoria said.

She fitted the new tube inside her tyre, tucked the valve through the rim hole, and worked the bead back on with her thumbs. The hand pump took long, patient strokes, and the tyre grew firm. When she squeezed it, the rubber gave nothing back. Ms. Santos-Reyes wandered over from the office with coffee, glanced at the wheel, and nodded once before walking back toward the cones.

Victoria spun the wheel and watched it blur. "Race you to the far end of the lot."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
The moving truck had pulled away two weeks ago, and Jayden still caught himself turning toward the corner where Yosef used to wait for the bus. Now he stood alone at the edge of the cafeteria at his new school, holding a tray of lasagna that smelled like burnt cheese. "You're in my seat," said a kid with a bowl cut and a dinosaur hoodie. "There are eleven empty seats," Jayden pointed out. "Yeah, but that one has the best view of the clock." Jayden moved one seat over. It was, in fact, an equivalent view of the clock.

At his old school, he and Yosef had done everything together, and the last night before the truck came, they had sat on the porch with Yosef's laptop. "Here's the thing," Yosef had said, slapping the screen. "Friendships fade if you don't keep in touch. The ones who stay close after moving are the ones who call and text regularly. So we're doing a video call every Friday at four. No excuses." He had typed it into a shared calendar, and Jayden's dad had laughed from the doorway and said, "Put me down for zero excuses too." They had both signed it, Yosef adding a doodle of a stick figure shouting into a phone.

The first Friday call had lasted ninety seconds because Yosef's little brother kept yelling about a lost sock. The second Friday, Jayden almost skipped it after a brutal day of dodgeball in gym, his arms heavy with fatigue, but he dragged himself to his room and logged on anyway. Yosef held up a slice of pizza. "Equivalent dinner to what we used to get at Sal's?" Jayden studied it. "Not even close. That's triangle sadness." They laughed until Yosef's mom told them to stop hogging the wifi.

At the new school, Jayden started testing an idea. He noticed the kids who seemed happiest at lunch were the ones pulling out phones, firing off messages, or planning weekend visits with friends from their old towns. The quiet ones who said "I lost touch with everyone" sat hunched like they were trying to insulate themselves from the whole room. So when the dinosaur hoodie kid, whose name turned out to be Fynn, mentioned he used to live three towns over and never talked to his old best friend anymore, Jayden said, "Why not?" Fynn shrugged. "It's been a year. It'd be weird." "My friend Yosef says it's only weird if nobody makes the first move," Jayden said, and felt like he was quoting a sacred text.

On the third Friday, Jayden set his phone against his math textbook and propped the door open with his sneaker so the wifi wouldn't stutter. Yosef appeared on screen with Fynn hovering behind him at his own house, because Fynn had texted his old friend that Tuesday and gotten a reply within an hour. "Told you," Yosef said smugly. Then Ms. Gupta, the neighbor who watered her tomatoes even in October, knocked on the doorframe. "Is that a three-way call? Make it a four-way," she said, holding up a clipboard covered in sticky notes. "I've got bingo night to organize." Yosef leaned closer to his camera and grinned. "Ma'am, you're already on the calendar."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Eli sat on his grandmother's porch with a clipboard on his knees, drawing her street for art class. The assignment was one-point perspective: the road had to narrow toward a single dot, the vanishing point, and every sidewalk edge and roofline had to run straight at it. He had done the road. He had done the dot. Now he was stuck on the hardware store across the street, because he could not decide which way its windows went.

Last summer, before the assignment existed, he had lain on this same porch with his grandfather, watching heat shimmer over the asphalt. His grandfather had pointed at the row of shops and said the street was older than the whole neighborhood, that everything new seemed to revolve around it, stores and schools and even the bus route. Eli had mostly been watching a dragonfly. But he remembered the storefronts themselves, flat and calm, like a stage set waiting for actors.

Aminata rode up on her bike and dropped her own homework on the porch beside him. Her drawing showed the same street, same dot, same narrowing road. Every line on her shop fronts was slanted, window tops running downhill toward the vanishing point, doorframes leaning like trees bent by tundra wind. Her buildings looked as if they had all agreed to tip over in the same direction.

"Mine looks wrong," she said, in the voice of someone who already knew and was hoping to be told otherwise.

"You slanted the fronts," Eli said. He did not say they looked like a landslide with awnings.

"The lines have to go to the point. That's the whole rule."

Eli held his pencil up at arm's length and sighted along the real hardware store across the street, one eye closed, the pencil held flat. The tops of its big front windows sat perfectly level against the horizon. The doorframe stood perfectly upright. He checked the bakery, the pharmacy, the shuttered laundromat. Level, level, level. The slanted lines were the ones running away from them, the sidewalk edges, the roofline stretching down the block.

"The fronts face us," he said slowly. "They're not going anywhere. In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical. Only the sides zoom off to the dot."

Aminata took her eraser and went at the leaning buildings. Eli traced two light guide lines across his own paper, one flat, one straight up and down, and hung the hardware store's windows on them like laundry on a line. When he looked up, his grandmother was watching from the screen door through its translucent mesh, holding two glasses of lemonade and saying nothing at all.

"Yours looks like a real street," Aminata said, squinting at his page. "Mine looks like an earthquake."

"Draw the fronts flat and save the earthquake for the alley," Eli said, and reached for a glass.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The moving truck was two cars ahead of them on the highway, and Emma watched it the whole time, as if it might do something. Their own car was crammed with suitcases, a cooler, and the last box from her room, the one she'd packed at midnight because the move had suddenly felt imminent, like weather you can see coming down the street.

She had her phone open to a page she'd found three days ago, when she couldn't sleep. "Listen to this," she said. "A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend."

"Fifty hours," her dad said, eyes on the road.

"That's like a hundred lunches. Maybe more, since lunch period is only half an hour if you count standing in line." She did the math on her knee. "A hundred school days. That's basically Christmas before anyone in the new school is even a casual friend."

Her little brother, wedged between the cooler and the suitcases, said, "Then don't be casual. Skip to best friend."

"It doesn't work like that," Emma said, and then she stopped, because she wasn't sure it didn't. She opened her messages. Uriah had sent eleven since morning, mostly pictures of their empty spot at the lunch table. Yasmina had sent a voice note Emma hadn't played yet, because once she played it she'd have to answer it.

Here was the thing she'd been chewing on for three days. With Uriah and Yasmina she already had the hours, years of them, banked like anything. If the 50-hour rule was real, then distance didn't delete the hours. It just meant nobody new had them yet. She could test that. She pressed record.

"Yasmina. Question. If I call you every day after school, like actually call, not text, does that count toward the fifty hours, or do you have to be in person?" She paused. "I'm going to cite you the study later. Dad, is Ashfield older than Riverton?"

"Ashfield? Much older. Started as a river settlement, back when the boats still came through."

"So people showed up knowing nobody, and they just stayed until the hours added up," Emma said, mostly to herself.

The truck's blinker came on. Exit 19, the sign said, and underneath it the name of the town that was now going to be on her library card and her gym shirt. Her dad slowed. The exit ramp was longer than she expected, curving past a water tower, a gas station, a strip of stores she'd never learned the names of.

Her phone buzzed against her knee. Yasmina, live, not a voice note: "Calling counts. Calling so counts. Tonight, 7:00. Don't be late."

Emma typed back one word, then put the phone face down on the box from her room as the car rolled up to their new street. "There's the truck," her brother said, pointing.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In France, friends often greet each other with cheek kisses called 'la bise', and the number of kisses varies from region to region.
story:
The door of Tante Margot's apartment opened at four o'clock, and Alexander stepped into a wall of perfume, piano music, and about eleven relatives he had never met. His family had flown in from Ohio for the reunion, and his mother had whispered one warning on the stairs: "Whatever you do, greet everyone properly." That was all she said before vanishing toward the kitchen.

His cousin Benoît came first, tall and grinning, and planted two quick kisses near Alexander's cheeks, one on each side. "Welcome," Benoît said. "We call that la bise." Alexander managed a nod, cheeks burning, and filed the move away: two kisses. Simple. He could do two kisses.

Then Grand-mère Odile swept in from the balcony and gave him three, left cheek, right cheek, left, before he had even finished saying bonjour. Alexander stood very still while she pinched his shoulder and said something rapid and delighted. Three. Not two. Behind her, the afternoon sunlight refracted through a crystal decanter on the sideboard and threw tiny rainbows across the tablecloth, and Alexander stared at those spots of light as if they might hold an answer.

He retreated to the hallway to think. Two kisses from Benoît, three from Grand-mère. If he did the wrong number, would someone be offended? He needed a rule, and he needed it fast, because Tante Margot was already calling that dinner, the whole reunion dinner, would be served at six o'clock sharp, and before that he would have to greet at least six more relatives, including Great-Aunt Sylvie, who according to Benoît "notices everything." Alexander had fewer than two hours.

He texted Rowen, back home, who knew nothing about France. No help. So he tried an experiment instead. He found Benoît and, with his most casual face, asked him to introduce him to Uncle Pierre. Alexander counted under his breath as Uncle Pierre greeted him. Two kisses. Then he tagged along to the balcony, where Cousin Anouk was setting out chairs. Anouk gave him three. Alexander added the data up in his head. It wasn't about age, and it wasn't about how well you knew someone, because Uncle Pierre barely knew him and still did two, the same as Benoît. The pattern seemed to run in the family itself, certain relatives doing two, certain relatives doing three, as if they'd each learned it wherever they'd grown up. When he tested it once more on Benoît's younger sister and got two, matching Benoît exactly, he felt the rule click into place: watch the family, not the person.

At five minutes to six, Great-Aunt Sylvie arrived, small and sharp-eyed, with a look that Alexander would have described as predatory if a butterfly were doing it. He offered his cheeks and held still, watching nothing, feeling for the rhythm. One, two, three. She drew back and smiled for the first time all evening.

"Smart boy," she said, and steered him toward the plateau of cheese at the center of the table.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard ticked toward fourth period, and Nathaniel's program still hadn't finished checking whether 9973 was prime. He pressed Enter again, watching the cursor blink. "It's just sitting there," he whispered.

"That's the gradual part," said Jeremiah from the next computer. "Mine took three minutes for a four-digit number. I timed it. I ate half a granola bar waiting."

Mr. Mwangi had appointed Nathaniel as the one to demo the prime checker at the coding showcase on Friday, which meant Nathaniel's program could not stand in front of the whole school eating granola bars while it thought. He needed it fast, and he needed it before Friday.

Isis leaned over from her seat. "Show me your loop."

Nathaniel turned his monitor so she could see. His program asked for a number, checked if it was divisible by 2, and then, if the number wasn't divisible by 2, it tested every single divisor up from 3 anyway. Four, five, six, seven. "It's checking everything," he said. "Even numbers, odd numbers, all of them."

"Why check four?" Isis asked.

"Because it's there?"

"Is your number even?"

"No. It wasn't divisible by 2, or it would have stopped."

Isis spun her pen once and caught it. "So it's odd. Can an odd number ever be divided evenly by an even one?" Nathaniel started to answer and then stopped. He tried it in his head. Nine divided by four. Twenty-five divided by six. Fifteen divided by eight. Every answer came out with something left over, every time. "No," he said slowly. "It can't."

"So after the check for 2," Isis said, "you only need to test odd divisors."

Nathaniel deleted the line that moved his counter up by one and replaced it with a line that moved it by two. Three, five, seven, nine. Half the work, gone. He saved the file with a dramatic click, like a judge sealing a verdict.

Jeremiah had been watching over his shoulder, chin propped on his fist. "Run it. Run it right now. I want to see 9973 lose."

Nathaniel typed 9973 and pressed Enter. The verdict appeared before the cursor finished its first blink. PRIME, said the screen, as if it had never been slow a day in its life.

"Two seconds," Jeremiah said. "Maybe less. My granola bar is irrelevant now. I'll have to find a new snack strategy."

Isis laughed, then nudged Nathaniel's arm. "Put a really big one in. Like, a monster."

He typed 104729, a number he'd seen on a poster in the math hallway, and held his breath. The screen thought for a moment, one long moment, and printed PRIME.

Mr. Mwangi wandered over from the window and read the screen. "Six digits," he said, eyebrows up. "On Friday, when the principal asks how it works so fast, what will you tell her?"

Nathaniel looked at his loop, at the little jump by two, and grinned. "I'll tell her we made the program twice as lazy, and twice as fast."

"Perfect," said Mr. Mwangi. "Save your file twice. Twice as lazy, twice as careful."

Nathaniel clicked save, then clicked it again, and the little green checkmark blinked at him twice.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing.
story:
Emilie spread her draft across her grandmother's kitchen table, between a bowl of plums and a vase of zinnias cut that morning. The assignment was due Monday: a short story with dialogue and a clear climax, and Mr. Çelik had written "check your punctuation" beside her first attempt in red pen. Her grandmother set down a glass of lemonade and peered over her shoulder without saying anything, the way she did when she wanted Emilie to figure things out for herself.

The line giving her trouble was this one: "Stop," Mom said. "Pulling the rope so hard." It looked like two separate sentences to Emilie, but when she read it aloud, she heard one sentence broken in half. She frowned at the capital P. Something about it felt wrong, like a door hung crooked on its hinges.

She tried an experiment. She covered the middle of the line with her thumb so only the quote showed: "Stop pulling the rope so hard." One sentence, smooth and whole. When she lifted her thumb, the tag sat in the middle like a stone in a stream, splitting the flow but not stopping it. So the second part was still the same sentence, just interrupted. It should begin with a lowercase letter. She erased the capital P and wrote a small one instead, then did the same to two other lines in her draft.

Her friend Kylan called that afternoon, and she read him the fixed line. "That's the one Mr. Çelik marked," he said. "When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part starts lowercase because the sentence is continuing. He told Ronin that on Tuesday." Emilie laughed, partly because she had worked it out on her own and partly because she had spent an hour doing what a five-second rule covered. "Can you paraphrase it for me anyway, so I know I have it right?" she asked, and Kylan put it in plainer words: if the tag breaks one sentence, keep it lowercase after the break.

The climax was the other problem. Her story about a girl rescuing a kite from a power line built slowly and then just ended, flat as a dropped pancake. Emilie read it to her grandmother on the porch that evening, cicadas droning in the hedges. "Everything is calm," her grandmother said. "Where is the moment everything changes?" Emilie realized she had been naive about endings, believing that if she described enough details, a climax would simply appear. Climaxes had to be built, the way her grandmother built the stone wall by the garden, one deliberate choice at a time.

She moved the moment the girl decides to climb instead of calling for help to the top of the last page, made the wind louder, made the choice cost something, and let the dialogue carry the peak of the tension. "Hold the ladder steady," Mom said, and the whole story turned on that lowercase continuation, the sentence rushing on just like the girl, refusing to stop.

At school on Monday, Mr. Çelik read the page, looked up, and slid it back with a single word written at the top. "Better," Emilie read, and grinned all the way to her seat.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The noon Sun climbs higher in the sky in summer than in winter, so shadows at noon are shorter in summer.
story:
Lucas had one week to build a model that explained the seasons, and his group had left him alone with a Styrofoam ball and a flashlight. "You're the science guy," Ivan had said, backing toward the door of the science room. "I'm the guy who makes posters look exceptional. That's my gift." Ivan's want was simple: a poster good enough to hang in the hallway showcase, which had never once featured his work. Lucas wanted something different. He wanted to actually understand the thing, not just recite it.

The trouble was that Earth's tilt was invisible. You couldn't watch it happen. He could speculate all evening about angles in space, but speculation felt like guessing with better vocabulary. He needed something on the ground, something he could measure. Then he remembered the fence post behind the gym, the one with a crooked top like a bad haircut. Shadows. Shadows were the tilt leaving fingerprints.

At lunch he dragged Sara outside. "Hold this ruler," he said. "At noon exactly, we measure the post's shadow." Sara squinted at the sun. "This is for a grade, or are you starting a shadow collection?" "Both," Lucas said. "It's going to be an exceptional collection." The shadow at noon that day in December stretched long across the icy grass, longer than the post itself. Sara wrote the number on her palm with a pen because paper would have blown away.

Lucas found a photo on the classroom computer from June, a class picnic, and there was the same post in the background. At noon, its shadow was a short dark stamp in the grass, barely a step long. He sat back so fast he nearly rolled the chair into Ms. Bouchard's supply cart. The noon Sun must climb higher in the sky in summer, he thought, because that was the only way a shadow could shrink like that. Same post, same time of day, different height in the sky. It wasn't a trick of the eye. It wasn't an illusion. It was a pattern, and patterns had causes.

He wrote a note and folded it into a paper airplane, which was against at least two rules, and sailed it to Ivan's desk. "Dear Poster Guy," it read. "Draw the same fence post twice. June: tiny shadow, sun high. December: giant shadow, sun low. Label both NOON. Then people can see it, not just hear it. Also, I owe you a cookie. Negotiable. Signed, Science Guy." Ivan wrote back on the same paper: "Cookie is non-negotiable. Also my poster is going in the showcase. Deal?"

On presentation day, the flashlight beam hit the tilted ball at an angle while Sara moved a cutout sun from low to high behind it. "Watch the shadow," Lucas said. "Short in summer, long in winter. Same post, noon both times." A kid in the second row raised his hand. "So the sun's just higher in summer?" "At noon, yes," Lucas said. "Higher in summer, lower in winter. That's the whole show." Ms. Bouchard circled something on her clipboard, and Ivan, at the back, held up his poster with both hands like a championship sign. "Showcase," he whispered. "I can feel it."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Sebastian had until nine o'clock, and the clock on the stove said 7:42. Ms. Pérez had assigned each student a primary source and one criterion for judging it: the source had to explain, in its own words, why a real family went west on the trails in the 1800s. Sebastian had printed eleven pages from a scanned settler's diary, and so far he had written one sentence, which he had already crossed out twice.

He spread the pages across the kitchen table. The handwriting was cramped and faded, and half the ink had gone brown, which struck Sebastian as bizarre for something his teacher called a document rather than an artifact. He could read the weather reports fine. Rain again. Oxen restless. But every time he reached for the reason the family had left their old home, the diary went quiet about it, as if the writer thought it was obvious.

His phone buzzed. Lauriane had sent a photo of her own source, a newspaper advertisement, with the message, "Mine came with the reason in the headline. Lucky me." Sebastian typed back, "Mine came with oxen," and set the phone face down. He pulled the lamp closer and started reading the pages in order instead of hunting around, because hunting had gotten him nowhere for an hour.

Near the end of the second page he found it. "The bank took the farm in the spring of thirty-seven," the writer had scrawled, "and Papa says land out west is cheap and the soil is black as coffee. We would rather risk the trail than stay and owe." Sebastian sat back. Thirty-seven. He grabbed his laptop and typed the year and the word panic together, more on a hunch than anything, and there it was: the Panic of 1837 had caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers had later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land. The diary line wasn't just one family's bad luck. It was part of a crowd.

He wrote a paragraph arguing that the family had not gone west for adventure but because they had lost everything, and that the diary proved it better than a textbook could, because the textbook would say "economic forces" while the diary said "the bank took the farm." He checked the clock: 8:51. He was fine. He attached the file, hovered over submit, and read his paragraph once more to make sure his evidence actually backed his claim.

That was when the wifi bar dropped to nothing. Sebastian refreshed the page, then stood and carried the laptop toward the router in the hallway, walking slowly so he wouldn't jostle it, as though the signal might accompany him if he was gentle. From the kitchen his phone buzzed again. Lauriane's new message glowed on the table where he couldn't read it: "Wait, don't submit yet. Ms. Pérez changed the due date. It's tomorrow now." The router's light blinked red, then green, and the page finally loaded, his finger already resting on the button.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Ava sat at the kitchen table with her history notes spread in front of her, but she kept reading the same line about the British monarchy without taking any of it in. Tomorrow was the unit test, and beneath the worry about the test sat something heavier: her tryout results for the regional orchestra were being posted at five o'clock, and it was already four thirty.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Ariah: "You checking the list at five?" Ava typed back, "No. My mom's checking and texting me the second it's up." There was a long pause, then Ariah wrote, "You're making her do it? Bold." Ava stared at the words and understood what was underneath them. Ariah wasn't impressed. Ariah was saying, you're hiding.

"I can't watch the page load," Ava admitted. "My hands shake." Ariah replied with a single question mark, so Ava kept going. "It's not just nerves. It's like anxiety, the real kind, where your brain decides something terrible is happening even when nothing has happened yet." She pressed send before she could delete it. Confiding in someone, even over text, felt like opening a door she usually kept shut.

Dillon jumped into the group chat a minute later. "Ava, did you know that if you stare at the ceiling for exactly four minutes you absorb knowledge from your notes? Learned it last night." Ava almost laughed. "You think I'm gullible enough to believe that?" "Worth a try," Dillon wrote, and then, more seriously: "When I have a bad day I run laps until my legs are tired. Works better than staring at walls."

Ava looked at the clock. Four thirty-five. She thought about what she usually did after a bad day: sat in her room, replayed everything, and let the stress grow instead of shrink. That was one way of coping, maybe, but not a good one. Ariah's next message confirmed it. "Coping is basically whatever you do to handle stress or hard feelings," she wrote. "My sister taught me that. The healthy stuff is like running, sleeping enough, or talking to someone you trust. I talk to you, mostly." Ava read the line twice. Talking to someone. She was already doing that part.

She typed, "I'm going for a walk around the block before five. Tell Dillon his ceiling theory is under scientific review." Then she pulled on her sneakers, set her phone to silent, and stepped out into the cool evening air. The sky was pale gold over the rooftops, and a neighbour was watering tomato plants, and none of it had anything to do with orchestras or monarchies. By the time she rounded the corner, her hands were steady.

When she got back, the phone was lit up on the porch step. One message from her mother: a screenshot of the list. Ava made herself read the first line before anything else, the way you test an idea by trying it once. Her name was there, second from the top.

She called Ariah, who picked up on the first ring. "Second chair," Ava said. "I read it outside, standing up."

"See?" Ariah said. "Told you the fresh air was part of the plan."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Joining a club or team at a new school puts a student in regular contact with the same people who share an interest, which gives friendships time to grow.
story:
The removal truck left at noon, and by evening Penelope had unpacked only enough boxes to find her toothbrush. Maple Crescent was a strange street, all new asphalt and young trees tied to stakes, and from her window she could see the arid strip of dirt beside the driveway where nothing had been planted yet. In her old town she had Tiago two doors down and Donovan on the corner, and now there was nobody, just streetlights blinking on one by one.

She called Donovan that night anyway. "The problem is I won't see anyone," she said, lying on the bare mattress. "At my old school I saw you every single day whether we planned it or not. Here I'd have to knock on strangers' doors, and that's..." She trailed off, listening to him crunch chips on the other end.

"It's the worst," Donovan agreed. "But you're going to school somewhere, right?"

That was when the idea landed in her head, so clear she sat up. Friendship needed time, and time needed a reason to keep showing up. Random people at lunch changed every day, but a club met on a schedule, the same people, the same interest, over and over. She couldn't see a friendship before it existed, but she could see the structure that let one grow. It was like the stakes holding up those skinny new trees: invisible support until the roots took hold.

Monday at lunch she wandered past the cafeteria, where every table already had its history, and found the room where the chess club met. A boy with a lanyard looked up. "You play?"

"Badly," Penelope said, which was true, and she sat down before her conscience could talk her out of it. She lost three games that first day. She lost two the next Tuesday, and a girl named Ruth showed her how the knight fork worked, tapping the piece twice like it was a secret handshake. By the third week Penelope won a game against a quiet kid named Marcus, and he demanded a rematch, and losing the rematch somehow felt like belonging.

On Friday, Ruth waved her over to a table near the window, unprompted. "Saturday, my place, we're watching the tournament footage. Bring snacks." Penelope texted Donovan a photo of the chess room door, then put the phone face down on the table and set up the board. "Your move," she told Marcus.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
story:
The soup jar had been sitting on the back shelf of the counter for nine days, and it was bubbling like a witch's brew. Camille held it up to the window light and turned it slowly, while Kelly, on video call from her kitchen table, made a gagging noise into the phone.

"Don't knock it, that's my data," Camille said. She grabbed her notebook. Next to the bubbling jar sat its twin, a jar she'd sealed with tape the same afternoon her mom made the soup, and that one was clear and still. The science fair was in two days. She'd planned to build a model volcano, but Ms. Otieno had postponed the fair once already because of the snow, and now the whole gym was booked solid and Camille's volcano prototype had cracked down the middle in the cold garage. The jars were her new project, and she had exactly one working night left.

"Okay, so here's my hypothesis," she said out loud, writing it down. "If germs float in from the air, then an open jar goes bad and a sealed jar doesn't. That's a testable guess. The jars are the test, and they already kind of support it." Kelly said that sounded good, but Omer, who had been reading over Camille's texts in the group chat, was less optimistic. He typed: bad plan, microbes could already be IN the soup when it's made. Sealed jar would go bad too then. Your jars can't prove which it is.

Camille stared at the bubbling broth. He had a point. Both jars had the same soup, so if the sealed one had gone bad too, that would have overturned her guess. But it hadn't, so the air seemed to matter. Still, she wanted a way to catch the germs in the act, coming in.

She went digging through the science book Ms. Otieno had lent her, flipping pages at the counter while the soup burped softly behind her. Then she stopped. There was a picture of glass flasks with long S-shaped necks, and a paragraph about Louis Pasteur. He had boiled broth in those flasks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. The flasks were open to the air, but the bend caught everything before it reached the liquid.

Camille read it twice, then grabbed a fresh jar of soup and a bendy drinking straw. She taped the straw into the jar lid so it made a curvy neck, boiled the soup first like the book said, and set the whole thing beside the originals. "Kelly! I'm building an S-neck flask out of a straw!"

"So if your straw jar stays clean," Kelly said slowly, "the bend itself is trapping the germs, and the open jar proves it's the air, not the soup."

"Exactly. And if it goes bad anyway, my hypothesis is toast." Camille propped her notebook open to a fresh page titled Trial 3 and circled the date of the fair, twice.

The next morning she ran downstairs in her socks and skidded to a stop in front of the shelf. The straw jar sat there, pale gold and quiet, not a single bubble. She leaned in until her nose almost touched the glass, and behind her the front door opened with a clatter.

"Camille," her mom called, jingling keys, "the school just posted something about the fair, and you're going to want to see this."

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: Rinsing rice before cooking washes off loose surface starch, which helps the cooked grains stay separate instead of sticky.
story:
Florence stood at Mr. Bondarenko's stall with a shopping list in one hand and a bag of basmati rice in the other, doing math in her head. If the rice took twenty minutes, and the tomato curry took thirty-five, and the flatbread took four minutes a piece, she could start the curry first, then the rice, then roll the dough while everything bubbled. It was her first attempt at getting a whole meal to the table hot all at once, and Naomi and Mackenzie were coming to her house at six o'clock sharp to judge it.

"Rice, tomatoes, onions, flour," Mackenzie read over her shoulder. "What's the jar?" It was mango preserve, and Mackenzie held it up like a trophy. "Prestigious," she announced, pointing at the blue ribbon on the label. "Award winning. We're eating like champions tonight."

Mr. Bondarenko weighed her tomatoes and shook his head sadly. "I tried that curry last week," he said. "My rice came out like paste. One big lump. I had to eat it with a spoon like porridge." He pulled a photocopy of his own rice from his apron pocket, which he apparently kept to show people, and in the picture the grains sat in a sad beige brick.

Florence studied the photo. Her own rice at home had always come out fluffy and separate, grains sliding off the fork, and she had never thought about why. The difference, she realized, was the three minutes she spent swishing the rice in cold water before cooking, water going cloudy white each time she poured it off. "Did you rinse it?" she asked. Mr. Bondarenko blinked. "Rinse rice? It's already clean." Naomi gasped in mock horror. "Sir, you have to rinse off the loose starch on the outside, or all the grains stick together and go gluey." Mackenzie nodded solemnly. "Wash the starch away, and the grains stay separate. Everyone knows that. Even the pigeons know that."

At six o'clock, the kitchen smelled like onions and cumin, and Florence was dancing between three burners. The curry was thickening, the flatbread was puffing on the dry pan, and the rice, rinsed three times, steamed in its pot with a lid on. When her friends were finally seated, she lifted the lid and tilted the pot, and the rice tumbled out in separate grains, loose and shining, not one lump anywhere. Mackenzie applauded with a chunk of flatbread in each hand. Naomi spooned curry over her plate and said, "Mr. Bondarenko is going to cry when he sees this photo." Florence was already taking one, steam curling up in front of the lens. "Send it to him," she said. "Tell him the pigeons said hi."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Sophie sat cross-legged on the back step with her sketchbook, her pencil hovering over a half-finished drawing of a street. Serena sprawled on the grass beside her, fanning herself with a magazine while the air conditioner's turbine hummed behind the fence like a drowsy dragon. Sophie had promised Ms. Augustin she would bring a one-point perspective drawing to art class tomorrow, and right now her street refused to cooperate.

"I did everything," Sophie said, jabbing her pencil at the page. "The vanishing point, the road getting skinnier, the buildings leaning in. It still looks like a wall."

Serena leaned over. "You drew a street that runs straight at you, and it flattened itself like a pancake."

"That's not helpful." Sophie studied her drawing. The buildings looked okay, shrinking toward the dot where all her lines met. But the lampposts, that was the trouble. She had drawn every single one the same height, marching down both sides like soldiers. Same height, same gaps between them, all the way back. And somehow that was exactly what flattened everything, as if the lampposts were refusing to obey the street and had rebelled into a flat line, standing shoulder to shoulder in a predatory, no-nonsense row that swallowed all the depth she had built.

She flipped to a fresh page and tried an experiment, because the only way to beat a drawing was to test it. This time she made the nearest lamppost tall, nearly the height of a streetlight should be, and the next one smaller, and the next smaller still, shrinking them the way the road shrank. Then she squeezed the gaps tighter and tighter as they went, so the far ones huddled close together near the vanishing point. She held the page at arm's length.

Serena stopped fanning. "Whoa. It goes back forever. It's like a hallway that swallows the whole world."

"Objects of the same real size get drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are," Sophie said slowly, almost to herself, watching her own street open like a tunnel. "The lampposts are all really the same size. My eyes just needed the drawing to say so."

Then she frowned. She had never once walked to the end of her own street at dusk and actually counted how the real lampposts behaved. Sophie closed the sketchbook, tucked it under her arm, and stood.

"Where are you going?" Serena asked.

"To the corner," Sophie said. "I want to see if the street agrees with me."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The cultural festival filled the park with the smell of grilled corn and fried dough, and Adam had twelve dollars and one goal: try food from at least five booths before the drummers started at four. He was halfway through a skewer of spicy chicken when he heard Georgia's voice rise near the mural wall, sharp enough to cut through the crowd.

"You can't just decide that about somebody else," she was saying to Aarav. "That's the whole point."

Aarav crossed his arms. "I'm saying if her grandmother is from the community, then she's part of it. It's not complicated."

The "she" turned out to be a girl Adam had seen around school, someone who wore a beaded bracelet every day and had just tried to sign up at the Indigenous students' booth for the festival's storytelling circle. Someone at the booth had welcomed her. Someone else, Aarav had heard, had said she didn't count because her family hadn't lived on the reserve in two generations. Adam chewed slowly and listened. Who got to draw a line like that, and where did the pen come from? It seemed like the kind of rule that must be written down somewhere.

"Look it up," Georgia said. "I bet there's an actual answer."

Aarav pulled out his phone, thumbs moving fast. Adam leaned over his shoulder, still holding his skewer, and watched him search through UN documents until he found it. "Here," Aarav said, and read aloud: "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007." He scrolled. "It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership." The three of them stood quiet for a second, the drums starting up somewhere behind them.

"So the community decides," Adam said slowly, testing the idea the way you'd test ice on a creek. "Not outsiders. Not even her own grandmother, really. The peoples themselves get to say who belongs." He tried to assess whether that settled the argument or just moved it, because "the community" still meant people, and people could disagree. But at least now the disagreement would happen inside the group, where the pen actually belonged.

Aarav stared at the screen. "I was deciding for them," he said. "Both sides. I was sure I knew the answer for somebody else's community." He looked toward the storytelling booth, where the girl was laughing with the woman running it. "I'm going to go say I was wrong."

Georgia grinned. "Bring her a fry bread. It's the least venomous apology in the world."

"That's not what venomous means," Aarav said, already walking.

"It was worth a try," she called after him, and Adam followed, finishing his skewer, the drums getting louder with every step.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The protagonist is a story's main character, and the antagonist is the character or force working against them; their conflict drives the plot toward the climax.
story:
Alicia sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to page three, a pencil with tooth marks on the eraser end, and a story that had stopped moving. Her main character, a boy named Marcus, was supposed to be walking to his grandfather's house through a snowstorm, but he had been standing at the end of the driveway for two paragraphs. The assignment sheet from Mr. Joshi was taped to the wall above the table. It said the story needed correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax, due Friday.

Her brother kept opening the fridge and letting it hum, so she had retreated to the table by the window, where the radiator ticked. Talon knocked at the back door at four o'clock, stamping snow off his boots. He wanted to borrow the family sled before the hills turned to ice, which was his way of wanting everything the storm had to offer.

"Read it to me," Talon said, dropping into the chair across from her. "I'll tell you if it's boring."

"It's not boring. It's just stuck." Alicia read aloud. Marcus's older sister was supposed to be the villain, the one who refused to drive him. Every line of dialogue she had written for the sister came out flat, like a person doing a homework assignment of her own.

"The sister doesn't sound like a person," Talon said. "She sounds like a stop sign."

Alicia looked at her page. The sister had one job in the story, which was to say no, and the more no she said, the less real she got. Meanwhile the snow, which Alicia had only been using as weather, kept doing things. It filled the tire tracks. It turned the road into a white field. It made Marcus's grandfather's phone line crackle and go dead. Alicia sat back, and the pattern assembled itself the way a photo comes up in a tray of developer. The person wasn't fighting the sister. Marcus was fighting the snow, and the snow was winning, and that fight was the whole story.

"The protagonist is the main character," she said, mostly to herself, "and the antagonist is the character or force working against him. It doesn't have to be a person." She crossed out three lines of the sister's dialogue with one stroke. The sister could still say no, once, and then drive off, and the snow would take over the job of being the problem. The cumulative weight of it, inch by inch, would push Marcus toward the moment of choice: turn back or keep going. That was the climax, and now she could see where to put it.

She rewrote the scene from Marcus's perspective on the empty road, the storm swallowing the fences, the cold working into his sleeves. Her dialogue got simpler and easier to punctuate, because people in trouble speak in short bursts. "We'll see you tomorrow," the sister calls through the window, and then the phone line dies, and Marcus pulls his scarf up over his mouth and steps off the driveway.

Talon read the new pages while she waited, tapping the pencil against the table. "So the sister just leaves," he said. "That works. The snow's the real enemy." He put the pages down and picked up the sled rope. "Can I still take this?"

"Take it," Alicia said, and turned to a fresh page. The storm outside thickened against the window, and she wrote: "Marcus counted his grandfather's fence posts, though he could only see three."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
Aaron pushed his peas around the plate while Sloane, who lived three houses down and had a habit of showing up at mealtimes, stabbed at her chicken and said, "One hundred is perfect, right? Like a perfect score on a test. So why does my dad keep yelling about a hundred and fifty-eight point three?"

Aaron set down his fork. "A hundred and fifty-eight point what?"

"Point three. He's watching football in the other room. He says the quarterback has a perfect passer rating."

Aaron's mother murmured something about not shouting through walls, and Sloane's face went pink. Aaron slid the last roll across the table to her anyway, because she always got embarrassed right before she talked herself out of asking anything.

He thought while he chewed. "Passer rating," he said slowly. "It's not like a test. It combines a bunch of passing statistics into one number." He counted on his fingers. "Completions, yards, touchdowns, interceptions, probably. A whole game squeezed into a single score." Sloane frowned, so he elaborated: "Instead of saying he threw for this many yards and completed this many passes, they mash it all together and hand you one number."

"So the scale is zero to what?"

Aaron pulled out his phone under the table, which his mother pretended not to see, and searched. He read the screen twice. "Zero to a maximum of one hundred fifty-eight point three."

"That's ridiculous," Sloane said. "Who picks that?"

"Somebody who wanted it to seem objective, I guess. Like the number is scientific." Aaron tapped his fork against his glass. "But here's the thing. It's only one game. A guy could have a perfect rating for one afternoon and still be ranked tenth in the league, because rankings use the whole season. One number hides everything else."

Sloane's dad hollered from the living room, "He did it again! Perfect game!" and Sloane winced, then laughed.

"Wait," Aaron said. He stood up, carried his plate to the sink, and on his way past the doorway peeked at the television. The same quarterback was on the screen, and the graphic underneath read: CAREER RECORD, PLAYOFFS. Aaron walked back to the table and sat down, grinning.

"What?" Sloane demanded.

"Your dad's been yelling about a perfect passer rating all night," Aaron said. "But the stat on the screen says the guy's never won a playoff game. Zero for four." He nudged the butter dish toward her. "So the number says perfect, and the record says keep watching."

Sloane chewed her roll, staring at the kitchen doorway where the game noise drifted through. Then she said, "My dad's going to need more chicken."

"I'll get it," Aaron's mother said, already standing.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: Letting all the air out of the tube first makes the tyre loose enough to lever off the rim.
story:
The driving school on Miller Road ran car lessons on weekdays, but on Saturday mornings the practice lot belonged to Ms. Kaur's bike maintenance course, and today the cones were pushed aside to make room for six bicycles lying on tarps. Victoria crouched beside her own bike, a plastic tyre lever in her hand, trying to work it under the edge of the back tyre. It would not budge. Beside her, Zachery had already flipped his wheel off and was watching her struggle with polite sympathy.

"You have to get it under the bead," he said, which was no help at all, since Victoria could not even find anything that felt like a bead under all that taut rubber. She pressed harder. The lever bent, slipped, and pinched her thumb against the rim. Imogen, working on the far side of the tarp, looked up at the small yelp.

"Mine did that too," Imogen said. "For like ten minutes."

Victoria sat back on her heels and looked at the wheel instead of fighting it. The tyre was hard as a drum, still fully pumped from her ride over. Ms. Kaur had said a tube could hide a puncture too small to see, like an organism too small for the eye, and you had to find it another way. Victoria was thinking about hidden things when the idea arrived: maybe the tyre was fighting her because it was full. If letting the air out changed how it sat on the rim, the lever might actually fit.

She found the valve, unscrewed the little cap, and pressed the pin inside with the end of the lever. Air hissed out in a long, steady rush, and the tyre softened under her fingers until it went slack and wrinkled. She slid the lever under the edge again, and this time it slipped in like a spoon into soup. She worked it around the rim, and the whole tyre came loose and transformed from a stiff hoop into something floppy she could peel back with her hands.

"That's it?" Zachery said, leaning over. "You just let the air out first?"

"That's it," Victoria said. She pulled the punctured tube free and ran her thumb along it while Imogen held a tub of water ready. When a thin thread of bubbles rose from one spot, she marked it with chalk, patched it, and pumped the new air in until the tyre stood round and firm again. It took a moment of wobbling to seat the wheel back in the frame, but the axle clicked home and the quick-release lever tightened under her fingers.

Ms. Kaur came by as Victoria spun the wheel and watched it whirl without a wobble. "Legitimate repair," she said, and moved on. Victoria lifted the bike, rolled it across the lot between the cones, and called back over her shoulder, "Race you to the mailbox and back."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
story:
The lights died at seven, right in the middle of Payton's homework, and her mother lit the candles on the coffee table so the living room glowed like something from an old photograph. Payton stood in the kitchen doorway anyway, staring at the freezer she had just spent ten minutes supervising while her brother tried, twice, to open it for ice cream. "Nobody opens it," she announced. "Every time you open it, cold air falls out like water."

"Since when are you the freezer police?" her brother asked from the couch.

"Since Mom did a big grocery run last week and we still haven't filled it back up. It's only half full." Payton had read something once, on a poster at Ms. Yang's community centre, and now she turned it over in her mind like a puzzle piece. If the freezer were full, it would hold a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power. Half full, only about 24 hours, and that was only if the door stayed shut. She did the math out loud. "The power's been off for one hour. We have maybe 23 hours left before we have to cook everything or lose it."

Her mother poked her head in from the hallway, phone pressed to her ear. "The utility says possibly two days, honey." Two days. Past the 24 hours. Payton sank onto the couch between the candles and her brother, watching the flames bend whenever anyone breathed. Tomorrow they would be grinding frozen burger patties into a chili the size of a bathtub. Tomorrow the neighbours would hear about it, and half the street would show up with plates, because her mother could never say no to a crowd.

She texted Fynn, whose family lived three streets over. His reply came back fast: our freezer is PACKED. dad says ours is good for like 48 hrs. Payton smiled at the screen in the candlelight. Full freezer, 48 hours. Half freezer, 24. At least now she knew the rule, even if she'd learned it a few grocery runs too late. It felt like discovering that the dinosaurs were extinct only after agreeing to pet-sit one.

By noon the next day they had cooked all of it, and the street did smell like chili, and people did come with plates, and Payton stood in the doorway watching Fynn eat a second bowl on her front step. That part was almost worth it. Then the refrigerator hummed. The lights blazed on, the oven fan roared to life, and every bulb in the house seemed to shout at once. Twenty-two hours early. Her brother set down his spoon and stared into the kitchen, where the freezer, now empty except for two lonely bags of peas, sat humming with nothing left to save. "So," he said, "anyone want ice cream? I hear we can open it now."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
The box on the kitchen table had a bow on it, which was Mom's way of saying sorry for making her wait until thirteen. Lea turned the phone over in her hands, set it up in ten minutes flat, and by dinnertime she had joined the family group chat, where Dad had already posted a photo of the dog wearing sunglasses with the caption "Welcome to the future." She replied with a thumbs-up, a rocket, and a skull, which in her grade meant approximately "this is amazing."

For the next week she participated in three group chats, played a frog game until her thumbs ached, and discovered that if she checked the phone one more time, there was always one more time after that. She also discovered something she did not like: lying in the dark at 10:30, wide awake, staring at the ceiling while her body refused to shut down. This had never happened before the phone. She lay there Wednesday night listening to the rain and thinking that there had to be a reason, because she was not nervous about anything and she had not even had soda.

At school she ran a quiet experiment on her friends. "When you can't sleep," she asked Libby, "what do you do in bed?" Libby said she scrolled until her eyes hurt. Zakariya said the same, except he put on a blue light filter because his cousin told him to, and he fell asleep fine. "Melatonin," Zakariya said, tapping his temple. "That's the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening." Lea frowned. A pattern needed more than two people, so she texted her cousin, who admitted she scrolled in bed every night and had basically become a nocturnal raccoon. Three for three, plus one filter-user who slept fine. The phone light was the hidden culprit, and the blue kind seemed to be the problem.

That night she left the phone charging in the kitchen, facedown, like a sleeping beetle. She felt the absence of it the way you notice a missing tooth. But at 10:05 she was already drowsy, and by 10:20 she was out cold, dreaming about the frog game anyway, because brains are cheaters.

The next morning the family group chat had a message waiting: "Good morning, sunshine. You look like you slept." It was from Grandma, whose frail hands still typed faster than Dad's. Lea typed back, "New house rule. Kitchen is where phones sleep." Grandma sent a crown emoji and then, in a rare second message, "Does the dog's sunglasses count as a blue light filter?" Lea laughed so hard her cereal almost came out her nose, and Libby, who had been examining her sore ear in the bathroom mirror and muttering "never get cartilage pierced during basketball season," yelled through the door to ask what was so funny. "Grandma," Lea called back. "Take the phone out of your room tonight and you'll laugh this hard at seven a.m. too."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: A testimonial uses a famous or admired person to endorse something, even though that person may have no special knowledge about it and may be paid.
story:
Easton stood in front of the shoe store window at the mall, his nose almost touching the glass. The sneakers behind it were white and gold, with intricate lacing patterns crisscrossing the sides, and above them a poster showed Dario Frost, the best point guard in the league, frozen mid-dunk with the shoes glowing on his feet. Easton had saved eleven weeks of allowance for these, and today, finally, he had enough.

"They're the Frost Pro Threes," said Thatcher, who had tagged along and was currently eyeing a rack of keychains nearby. Thatcher's real mission was a keychain shaped like a rocket, but he only had three dollars, so he kept drifting back to look at it and then drifting away again. "Everybody on the team is getting them," he added. "Cyril already ordered his online."

"Everybody, huh," Easton said slowly. That was a lot of pressure, the feeling that if he was the only one without them, he'd be standing out in the wrong way. He pushed the door open anyway and walked to the display.

At the counter, he asked the cashier if the shoes came in size seven. She checked the back, and while Easton waited, he stared up at another poster of Dario Frost. In smaller print at the bottom, almost hidden, were the words "Paid Partnership." Easton read it twice. He turned to the cashier. "Does Dario Frost actually pick these shoes himself? Like, does he study them?"

She shrugged. "I just sell them, kid. The company decides who's on the posters."

Easton exhaled and looked down at his money, folded in his pocket. The shoes were still good shoes. But he suddenly pictured a meeting room somewhere, executives choosing a famous face, knowing that kids like him would see the poster and think the choice was Frost's, when really Frost might be paid to say whatever they wrote. A famous person could admire the shoes, or he might know nothing about them at all, and the poster would look exactly the same. Easton thought about how that worked, testing it in his head like a math problem, and the answer surprised him: the ad only felt like proof.

"That's a testimonial," said a voice behind him. Mr. Kaur, his neighbor, was at the mall buying socks and had stopped when he saw Easton. "A famous face selling something," Mr. Kaur said, holding up his little bag. "Doesn't mean he knows a thing about it."

Easton bought the shoes anyway, because they fit and he'd saved for them. But he walked out saying, "Next time I'll figure out if I actually want it before I look at whose face is on it." Thatcher came out a minute later, holding the rocket keychain; the cashier had let him have it for three dollars and a promise to sweep the store's entrance mat on Saturday. "Trade you a look at my rocket for a look at your shoes," Thatcher said, spinning it on its little chain.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
Elliot stood at the door of the gymnasium with his hands in his pockets and counted the steps from the doorway to the DJ booth. Thirty-two. The speakers were stacked on either side of the booth like two giant gray lockers, and even from the door the bass thumped against his chest. Aila waved him over to where she and Conan were standing near the bleachers, and Elliot noticed something as he walked: the music got louder with every step, and the kids closest to the booth were shouting into each other's ears.

Last summer, Elliot had gone to a concert with his uncle, and afterward, in the quiet car, he had heard a thin whine in both ears, like a mosquito trapped somewhere near his brain. He had mentioned it at breakfast the next morning, and his uncle had said it happened to him too, and that it was called tinnitus, and that when your ears rang after loud music, it meant they had been hit by noise loud enough to damage hearing. His uncle had shrugged and said his own ears had stopped ringing by noon. But Elliot had lain awake that night listening for it, wondering whether it would ever stop.

At the dance, he tried to persevere through three songs near the front, because Aila and Conan were there and it was easier to dance in a crowd than alone. But he kept thinking about the thirty-two steps, and about the kids pressed right up against the speakers, and finally he tapped Aila's shoulder and pointed toward the back wall. She shook her head, defiant, her ponytail whipping as she kept dancing, so Elliot walked back alone.

From the doorway the music was still loud but his chest didn't shake. He could hear the separate sounds again, the hi-hat and the bass, instead of one giant blur. Conan wandered over a few minutes later with a paper cup of punch. "You look like you're guarding the exit," Conan said.

"I'm guarding my ears," Elliot said. He nodded toward the booth. "My uncle calls it tinnitus when they ring after loud music. It's a warning that the noise was loud enough to damage your hearing."
