Conan drained his punch and looked at the speakers, then at the kids beside them, then at his own empty cup as if it might offer an opinion. "So how close is too close?"

Elliot didn't know exactly, and he said so. But he had an idea, and he decided to test it. The next slow song, he walked halfway across the gym, stopped at the free-throw line, and held up his phone with the sound meter app his uncle had shown him. The number on the screen was lower than the reading he'd taken near the booth ten minutes ago, and he wrote both numbers on his hand in pen.

When Aila finally joined them at the back, sweaty and grinning, she leaned in to be heard. "Next dance, we bring the whole group back here," she said, and Elliot nodded and wrote 16 steps on his palm, right under the numbers.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: The brain's main reward pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area, deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens, and addictive drugs boost dopamine along it.
story:
Elena spread the brain diagram across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with a salt shaker, a mug, and two forks, because the paper kept curling. Her health project was due Thursday, and the assignment said she had to explain, out loud, how nicotine hooks people. "You can't just read the poster to us," Ms. Menon had said. "You have to make us understand it." Elena had labeled the diagram last night, but when she tried to say it aloud this morning, the words slid away from her like water off a pan.

Jaxx arrived first, letting himself in through the back door the way he always did, and dropped his backpack on a chair. Sharon came two minutes later, still holding half a granola bar. "Okay," Elena said, "you're my practice class. Ask me anything. Be mean about it."

She pointed at the diagram. "So the brain has a reward pathway, and it runs from the ventral tegmental area, deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens." Jaxx leaned in and squinted at her labels. "Which one's the ventral whatever?" Elena tapped a small oval near the middle of the drawing. "This. And nicotine boosts dopamine along that pathway." Sharon chewed her granola bar slowly. "What's dopamine feel like? Like, if I got some right now?"

That was the problem. Elena couldn't show them dopamine. She couldn't show them the pathway either, because it was buried inside a skull, and no one in her kitchen was volunteering to open one. She stood there holding a fork, thinking that this was the whole difficulty of her project: the most important part of it was invisible. "Okay, new plan," she said, and pulled the kettle off the counter and set it at the back of the table. "This is the ventral tegmental area." She put the sugar bowl near the front edge. "This is the nucleus accumbens." She took the long wooden spoon and laid it down between them. "This is the pathway. When something good happens, dopamine travels along it, kind of like water running down this spoon."

Jaxx frowned at the spoon. "That's the wrong direction." Elena looked. He was right; she had the kettle and the sugar bowl on the same side, so her pathway ran nowhere. "That's a contradiction," Sharon said, pointing between the diagram and the table. "Your poster says the pathway goes from deep in the brain to the nucleus accumbens, but your kitchen version goes sideways." Elena's face went hot. She moved the sugar bowl to the far end and repositioned the spoon so it ran from the kettle straight to it. "The pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens," she said again, slower this time, and this time she could see it.

"Fine, but why does nicotine make it addiction instead of just feeling good?" Sharon asked. Elena picked up the honey jar and tipped a thin stream onto the spoon, letting it run the whole length. "Nicotine boosts dopamine along the pathway. The brain keeps getting more than it should, so it wants it again and again. That's the addiction part." Jaxx watched the honey crawl toward the sugar bowl. "And that's why my uncle says quitting is like fighting something corrosive, like it eats at him from inside." He said it quietly, not like a joke, so nobody laughed.

Sharon suggested they boycott the kettle and sugar bowl during snack time, and Elena laughed for the first time all afternoon. They ran the explanation twice more, Jaxx playing Ms. Menon and asking annoying questions like "Are you sure it's not the nucleus accumbens to the ventral tegmental area?" while Sharon poured the honey again and again. By the third run, Elena could say the whole thing with her eyes closed, her finger tracing the air from deep in the invisible brain to its destination. When her mom got home and asked what they'd done all afternoon, Elena pointed at the honey-sticky spoon lying on the table. "I taught them the brain's reward pathway," she said, "and nobody even had to open their head."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
Ella had begun to dread the afternoon swim block at Camp Winook, because that was when Derek and his friends noticed Sonny's crooked dive and turned it into a joke. Today they were at it again, shouting " Belly flop!" before Sonny even left the board, and the whole dock seemed to snicker along with them.

Ella sat on the dock with Loralie and watched, chewing the strap of her goggles. She had been keeping a little tally in her notebook all week, mostly out of boredom, marking down every time the teasing happened and who was nearby. Almost every single time, other kids had been watching. There had been one anomaly, a Tuesday morning when the dock was empty except for Derek, and he hadn't said a word to Sonny at all. She flipped back through the pages. Eight times out of nine, the dock had been crowded.

"That can't be a coincidence," she said, showing Loralie the tally. "It's like he needs the audience." That night in the craft cabin, she found a page in an old camp counselor manual Mr. Henry had left on the shelf, and read a line out loud to Loralie: "A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes." Eighty-eight percent. Her notebook said eight out of nine, which was almost exactly the same thing.

"So it's not just Derek," Loralie said slowly. "It's everyone standing around letting it be a show."

The next afternoon, Ella tried an experiment. When Derek started up before Sonny's dive, she didn't yell at him, because last time she had tried that, it had only made him louder and Sonny redder. Instead she stood up, walked to the edge of the dock, and said, "Sonny, show us the arms thing you practiced." Loralie jumped up too, and two boys from the canoe group drifted over to watch Sonny instead of Derek. The joke sagged. Derek looked around for his audience and found everyone facing the other way.

It didn't fix everything. The cumulative effect of a whole summer of teasing didn't vanish in one afternoon, and Sonny still climbed the ladder with his eyes down. But at the top he paused, glanced at Ella, and said, "The arms thing looked okay, right?"

"Better than okay," Ella said. "Again?"

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it needs less pressure to cut, so it is less likely to slip off the food.
story:
At the farmers' market, Ms. Cho had one rule for the cooking demo: sauce done by noon, when the judges wandered through. Harper had forty minutes, a pile of onions, a cutting board wobbling on a folding table, and a knife she suspected had never once been sharp.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Ms. Cho said, demonstrating. "Knuckles guide the blade. Fingertips stay safe."

Harper copied the grip. It felt strange, like her hand was a small armored animal, but her fingertips vanished behind her knuckles just like Ms. Cho's. Then she set the blade against the onion and pushed. The knife mashed instead of slicing, and when she leaned harder, it skated sideways off the onion and clattered against the board.

"Whoa," said Samson, who had wandered over from the honey stall with a toothpick in his mouth. "You almost became a protagonist in a safety video."

"Funny," Harper muttered. She tried again, pressing with all her weight. The blade slid off again, and this time it nicked the tomato she'd set aside, tearing the skin rather than cutting it.

She stared at the wobbling edge of the onion, thinking. The knife wasn't biting in. It needed her whole body weight behind it, and all that force had nowhere to go except sideways when it slipped. A sharp knife would need barely any pressure at all. Less pressure meant less chance of sliding off the food entirely. That had to be why Ms. Cho's cuts looked so easy.

"Ms. Cho, can I borrow your knife? Mine's dull."

Ms. Cho handed it over without a word, which Harper appreciated. The new blade sank through the onion skin on the first gentle stroke, clean as a zipper. She kept the claw grip, let the knuckles guide the steel, and the slices fell away in tidy half-moons.

"How," Samson said.

"Sharp knife. Barely have to push." She said it like a discovery, because it was.

Mathilde appeared at a run, breathless. "Judges are early. Twenty minutes, Harper."

The onions hit the pan and the sizzle seemed to cease all other market noise for a second. Mathilde stirred, Samson fetched basil from the herb stand, and Harper crushed the tomatoes with her hands, seeds and juice sliding through her frail, onion-stung fingers into the pot. The sauce bubbled, thickened, and smelled like an actual kitchen instead of a folding table.

Ms. Cho tasted it, then held out the spoon to the first judge walking up.

"Made by the tall one with the bandaged-free fingers," she said. "Notice the claw grip."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Lincoln sat on the floor of Kyan's bedroom with Kyan's phone in his hand, waiting for the science project page to load. Kyan was downstairs getting snacks, and Joanne leaned over Lincoln's shoulder, chewing the end of her pen. "Search my name," she said suddenly. "I did it once at my grandma's and nothing came up."

Lincoln typed her full name into the search bar and hit enter. Three results down, between a lawyer in another state and a gymnast from Canada, was a comment on a neighbourhood news site. The username was jojojoanne2019. The comment read, "The new playground by the river is way better. We go every Tuesday after swim." It was posted three years ago, when Joanne was nine.

"That's mine," Joanne said. She grabbed the phone and stared at it. "I forgot I ever wrote that. That site doesn't even exist anymore, I think. How is it still here?"

Lincoln scrolled up and checked the top of the page. The little green address was some archive thing, a copy of the old site. "It got saved somewhere," he said. "Somebody copied it." He was doing quiet reasoning in his head: if the site was gone but the page still existed, then something must have taken it before it disappeared. He wanted to know what.

Kyan came back with a bowl of pretzels and peered at the screen. "My cousin told me about this," he said. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers. They go around copying public pages."

"So it took a picture of my comment," Joanne said, "and now anyone can find it." She sounded more curious than upset, but Lincoln noticed her thumb tapping the corner of the phone case, over and over. The comment said every Tuesday after swim. The river playground. Their whole town.

Lincoln had an idea. He typed his own name into the search bar. His heart did a small jump while the results loaded. Nothing came up except a Lincoln from Ohio who sold tractors. He had never posted anything public; everything he did was on apps where only his friends could see it, and his username was a made-up word that had nothing to do with his real name. "See, that's the difference," he said. "Mine's not out there."

"Because you never put it out there," Joanne said. She took the phone back and opened the archive page, hunting for a delete button. There wasn't one. She tried the news site itself and got an error page with a sad little cartoon pigeon on it. Finally she abandoned the search, set the phone face down on the carpet, and took a pretzel.

Lincoln picked the phone up again. "Do the test," he said. "Search something you never wrote. Like, 'Joanne river playground Tuesday.'" He typed it in. The same comment surfaced at the top. Then he searched only "river playground Tuesday" and it appeared again, fourth result, still with her username beside it. The words in the comment had been indexed too, like labels on a shelf. Joanne watched the screen with her chin on her knees.

"So from now on," she said slowly, "I use words that don't point straight at me. No name, no place, no Tuesday." She held out her hand for the pretzel bowl, and Kyan passed it over. Outside, a lawn mower droned up the street, and the science project page still sat open behind everything, patient and forgotten. Lincoln closed the search tab and slid the phone across the carpet to Kyan. "Your turn," he said. "Search yourself before someone else does."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Each operation has an inverse that undoes it: subtraction undoes addition, and division undoes multiplication.
story:
Isla sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with her math binder open to a page that looked like it had been written in a foreign language. x + 7 = 12. Her grandmother had restricted her to one snack until the homework was done, which Isla felt was harsh, and the only snack allowed was oat bars, which her grandmother described as "low in carbohydrates and high in virtue."

Edouard and Aikam arrived on their bikes before Isla had written anything except her name. "Still stuck?" Edouard asked, dropping his helmet on the chair. "You were stuck on Tuesday too."

"I was not stuck on Tuesday," Isla said. "I was thinking in a very meticulous and organized way." Aikam stole an oat bar and chewed it with the face of someone doing math punishment.

Isla stared at the equation again. Some number was hiding under that x, and the 7 had been added to it. That was the whole problem, really. Something plus seven made twelve. She remembered fourth grade, when she had to guess how many cookies were in the jar after her cousin ate three, and she had figured it out by putting three cookies back. She had tested it even then, counting the jar after adding them, and it worked. Putting back was the opposite of eating.

"Subtraction is the inverse of addition," Isla said slowly. "It undoes it."

"Say what now?" Aikam said through the oat bar.

"If I take 7 away from both sides, the 7 disappears from the x side, and the 12 side becomes 5. So x is 5." She wrote it down, then tested it, the way she had tested the cookies. 5 + 7 = 12. It worked. She felt like she had picked a lock.

The next one was 3x = 15, and Isla stopped again. Edouard leaned over her shoulder. "Now what's hiding?"

"The x got multiplied by 3," Isla said. "So I need the thing that undoes multiplication." She thought of the jar again, cookies split evenly between three cousins. "Division. Divide both sides by 3." She worked it through. x = 5 again, which made her suspicious, so she checked: 3 times 5 was 15. Edouard checked it too, twice, because he did not trust the universe to be consistent.

"That's it?" Aikam said. "That's the whole chapter?" He picked up the pencil, did the next three problems without stopping, and slid the binder back. "I feel like we broke into somewhere we weren't supposed to be."

Isla closed the binder and reached for the oat bars. "Two snacks," she told her grandmother, who was watering the ferns by the window. "I earned two." She held one out to Aikam, who had eaten his already and was pretending he hadn't.

"One and a half," her grandmother said, and cut a bar in two with a butter knife.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Brooke had her whole science fair project planned out, and now the plan was falling apart in aisle nine of Hartley's Hardware. She needed a longer dowel, a new hinge, and enough time to rebuild her model wind gauge before Saturday. What she did not need was Giselle from school standing next to the bins of screws, telling her the project was doomed anyway.

"Ms. Szabó graded my poster rough drafts today," Giselle said. "She circled my whole question. I surveyed the sixth grade and kids who eat breakfast have higher grades, so I wrote that breakfast makes you smarter. She wrote 'Are you sure?' in red pen twice."

"So change the question," Brooke said, digging through the dowel bin like she could excavate the right length from the bottom of the pile. "Ask them more stuff. Ayman eats breakfast every day and he got a C on the last math quiz."

"That's one kid."

"It's a start."

They found Ayman himself by the paint samples, holding a swatch called Storm Cloud up to the light. When Brooke told him about Giselle's survey, he frowned. "My mom makes me eat breakfast because she's home in the mornings. On her early shifts, nobody's awake to make anything and I'm late anyway."

Brooke stopped with the dowel halfway out of the bin. "Wait. Say that again."

"My mom's schedule. When she works early, I skip breakfast and I'm rushed and I do worse on stuff."

Giselle pulled out her phone and looked at her own survey data. "Kids who answered 'always eat breakfast' also mostly answered 'parent home in the morning.' Almost all of them." She scrolled, and her shoulders dropped. "So maybe it's not the food. Maybe something else is behind both things."

"That's what Ms. Szabó meant," Brooke said. "Two things going together doesn't mean one causes the other. She called it correlation on the board last week and I zoned out, but it's this. Breakfast and grades move together, and something else could be pushing both."

"That's reckless, deciding breakfast is the cause off one survey," Ayman said, still holding his paint swatch like evidence. "My whole poster would've been wrong."

"Then your poster is about the real question," Brooke said. She pulled the right dowel free at last. "You show the numbers, and you say the honest thing: they go together, and you don't yet know why. Then you list what you'd check next." Giselle's face was still storm-cloud gray, so Brooke bumped her with the dowel. "Kids who rewrite their posters on Wednesday still make the fair on Saturday. That's another thing that goes together."

Giselle laughed and pocketed her phone. "Fine. But you're helping me make the new graphs."

"Deal," Brooke said, and headed for the register with her dowel held like a sword.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
Eva had saved eleven dollars for the blueberry jam she'd been craving for weeks, but when she reached Mr. Halloran's stall at the farmers' market, the small jars that used to cost four dollars now had a sign that said seven.

"Whoa," said Subhan, who had trailed along behind her with his canvas bag. "Did he make the jam out of gold this year?"

"Blueberries got hit by the late frost," Mr. Halloran said without looking up. "Half the growers around here lost their crop. This is all I've got." He gestured at the table, where only six jars stood in a neat little row, and behind Eva a line was already forming. A woman in a green coat bought two jars without even asking the price. Then a man bought one. Then two more vanished, and Eva's stomach tightened, because by the time she counted her money again, only one jar remained.

She bought it. Seven dollars, and she still clutched the jar like it was treasure as they walked on. At the next stall, a farmer had piled apples into a wobbly mountain, so many that a sign shouted "TWO DOLLARS A BAG, TAKE AS MUCH AS YOU WANT." Subhan bought a whole bag for the price of a candy bar. Eva turned the jam jar over in her hands, frowning, watching how the apple buyers barely had to queue at all. When almost nobody has a thing, the price climbs and people still fight over it. When there's too much of a thing, the price sinks. She could almost see the rule moving through the market like an invisible current.

Then came the honey stall, and the rule wobbled. The beekeeper's sign said twelve dollars a jar, triple last year's price, and Eva expected everyone to walk away. Instead the same people who had haggled over apples lined up without a murmur. A gray-haired woman bought three jars at once.

"I don't get it," Eva said. "It's even more expensive than the jam. Why does anyone pay that?"

"My mom takes a spoonful every single day," Subhan said. "Doctor's orders. She'd buy it at twenty dollars." He paused. "I heard my sister call that inelastic demand. For stuff people actually need, like medicine, the price going up doesn't change how much they buy."

Eva looked at the jam in her hand, suddenly glad it was a want and not a need, and glad she hadn't been gullible enough to believe the rumor that the whole market would restrict Saturday selling hours, an anecdote her little brother had sworn was true and which had turned out to be nothing.

"Well," she said, peeling off the lid, "some rules bend."

She held out the jar to Subhan. "Want the first taste?"

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: Some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason.
story:
Leo sat at the kitchen table with his notebook open to a blank page and a pencil he had already sharpened twice. The assignment from Mr. Wiśniewski was due tomorrow: a thesis statement plus an outline of a three-point argument, before any drafting. Leo had his topic, a petition to keep the school field open on weekends, but the three points sat scattered in his head like dropped marbles.

He texted Charlize because she had finished hers two days early. Her reply came as a message he read on the counter while the kettle hissed: "Mr. W read mine out loud as an example. Want to know the trick? Don't put your best reason first. Some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason. I ended on the money argument and it worked." Leo read it twice. His strongest point was that closing the field would fracture the neighborhood, since the weekend games were the only thing that brought everyone together. His weakest was that the grass was nicer than the parking lot the school wanted to build.

Benoit knocked on the door before Leo could decide, holding his own notebook and a bag of chips. He flopped into the chair across the table and slid his outline over. Benoit's want was simple and he said it out loud: he needed at least a B or his mother would take his bike for a week. His outline had one point written and two blank lines. "I always run out of reasons," he said.

"Give me your weakest one," Leo said, and pushed the chips aside to make room. He wrote his own outline while Benoit watched: first the grass, then the traffic danger of a new lot, and last, underlined, the neighborhood fracture. "Why save the best for last?" Benoit asked. Leo turned the phone so he could read Charlize's message. "Because the argument builds," Leo said, "and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason. Weak to strong."

Benoit copied the shape of it, weakest, middle, strongest, for his own topic about later start times. Leo thought about last year's essay on zoos, where he had fired off his best evidence in the first paragraph and then dribbled out weaker stuff for two pages. Maybe that was why Mr. Wiśniewski had written "fades" in the margin. Maybe Charlize's way would have carried it further. He couldn't decide, and the margin comment was still somewhere in his binder if he ever wanted to check.

He read his thesis aloud once, testing it against the outline like pressing on a fracture to see if it held. "Closing the weekend field would harm the school, the street, and the whole neighborhood," he said, and Benoit gave a vigorous nod through a mouthful of chips.

"Write that down before you forget it," Benoit said.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under first-past-the-post, two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, letting a third candidate win with fewer votes than their combined total.
story:
The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Charlie clutched her notebook like it was evidence. Her class was there to watch a mock election trial, part of Ms. Otieno's unit on how votes become power, and Charlie had one job: count the sample ballots. Lily had handed them over on the bus, sealed in an envelope, and made her promise not to peek until the demo started.

"You're the official counters," Ms. Otieno said in the hallway outside Courtroom Two. "Calum and Lily, you hand out the ballots. Charlie, you tally. Ready?"

Charlie was not ready. Two weeks ago, the eighth grade had held its real election for class rep, and the results still sat in her stomach like a swallowed stone. Calum had run on more recess equipment. Lily had run on fixing the broken basketball hoop. Nearly the same promise, worded two ways. And Rhea from the other homeroom, who wanted a candy vending machine, had won. Charlie had voted for Lily, and she still could not make the numbers line up in her head.

The demo began. Forty students and parents played the town of Ridgefield, voting for three imaginary council seats. "First, we count the old way," the clerk announced. "One round, and the top three win." Charlie sorted the ballots into piles. Purple Party, nineteen votes. Green Party, twelve. Orange Party, nine. She wrote the totals on the board, her marker squeaking.

Then the clerk said the word that had been sitting dormant in the back of Charlie's mind since the real election, waiting to wake up. "Now we redo it with proportional representation. Seats divided to match the share of votes." Charlie did the division, her logic grinding through it like her grandfather's old snow blower. Nineteen of forty won one seat plus a big chunk of another. Twelve and nine would not just vanish this time. But her pencil stopped. Because under the first count, the Greens and the Oranges, whose platforms were almost identical, had won nothing at all. Their voters had split between two similar choices, and Purples had taken everything with fewer votes than the two smaller parties combined.

Charlie flipped back a page in her notebook to the eighth-grade tally she'd copied off the bulletin board. Calum, forty-one. Lily, thirty-eight. Rhea, fifty-two. She stared until the numbers seemed to move. Calum and Lily's supporters had wanted the same thing, and together they had seventy-nine votes against Rhea's fifty-two. The split had let Rhea win. It had happened to them, right there in the gym, and nobody had seen it.

"Ms. Otieno," Charlie said, holding up her notebook, her voice louder than she meant it to be. "This is what happened to us."

Ms. Otieno looked at the page, then at the board, then raised her hand toward the clerk. "Could the counters present both results to the court?"

Charlie stood, walked to the rail, and turned the notebook around so the whole room could see the two columns of numbers, side by side.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, the % operator gives the remainder of a division, so n % d == 0 is true exactly when d divides n evenly.
story:
The computer lab smelled like warm keyboards, and Megan had exactly twenty minutes of lunch left to make her program work. She wanted it to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, because Mr. Chatterjee had promised that the first three finished programs would run on the big screen at the science showcase. Across the aisle, Ulysse was already typing fast, and he kept glancing over at her monitor, hoping she would get stuck so he could be first for once.

"I'm almost done," he said, though his screen was mostly empty. "Mine's going to be anonymous, no name on it, so when it wins everyone will wonder who wrote it." He wanted the mystery more than the prize itself, Megan could tell. She inheritance-typed faster.

Her problem was the middle of the program. She knew a prime had no divisors except one and itself, but the computer could not look at a number and see that. It had to test it, and she did not know how. She tried dividing: 15 divided by 3 gave 5.0. But 14 divided by 3 gave 4.666666666666667. The decimal went on and on, and comparing decimals felt fragile, like a bridge that might wobble. There had to be a better way.

"Try the percent sign," said Ulysse, leaning over, unable to resist showing off. "In Python, the percent operator gives the remainder of a division."

"A remainder," Megan repeated. Her conscience made her say, "You're not just inventing that to slow me down?" He shook his head so hard his headphones slipped. She typed it into a test line: 15 % 3 came out as 0, and 14 % 3 came out as 2. So n % d == 0 would be true exactly when d divided n evenly, and no decimals anywhere. That was it. That was the whole trick hiding inside the machine.

She built her loop, testing every possible divisor from 2 upward, and her fingers flew. Ulysse abandoned his anonymous plan entirely and scooted his chair next to hers, because now he wanted to see it work more than he wanted to win. Megan typed 91, pressed Enter, and held her breath while the cursor blinked.

"Not prime," the screen printed. Seven times thirteen. She threw her arms up, and Ulysse was already shouting, "Mr. Chatterjee, come look, come look!"

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
Isabella had been walking the stroller around the duck pond for twenty minutes, and the baby had been crying for every one of them. The neighbor's daughter, six weeks old and red-faced, screamed with her whole tiny body, and the sound bounced off the water and came back twice as loud. Tony was throwing bread crusts to the ducks with Prince, and Prince jogged over when he heard the crying change pitch.

"Just bounce her," he said, reaching toward the stroller. "Like, shake her a little, up and down. My cousin does that and the baby goes quiet."

"Don't." Isabella put her hand flat on the blanket, blocking him. "You can't ever shake a baby. Not even a little. Their neck muscles are too weak to support a heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury." She heard her own voice shake on the last word, because she was remembering the babysitting course in the church basement last spring, the video where a nurse said that exact thing while Isabella sat in a folding chair feeling sick to her stomach. She had thought the fact would never matter. Now it mattered.

"So what do we do?" Prince asked.

Isabella racked her brain. The baby wasn't hungry; the bottle had been finished at the neighbor's house before the walk. Her diaper was dry. She wasn't too cold in the June sun. That left something Isabella couldn't see directly, some hidden cause, and she ran through the possibilities like keys on a ring. Too much stimulation? The park was loud with ducks and a distant mower and kids on the swings. She tested the idea: she tipped the stroller seat back until the baby lay flat and safe, swung the canopy over to shade her, and steered away from the pond toward a quiet patch of grass under an oak.

"I need a minute too," she admitted to Prince, and she meant it, because the crying had been scraping at her nerves until she could feel herself resenting a six-week-old, which was unfair and she knew it. She stood three steps from the stroller, took a slow breath of cut-grass smell, and counted the loud cries. Then quieter ones. Then hiccups. Then, unbelievably, silence.

Mr. Yang, who kept his garden plot near the fence, looked up from his tomatoes. "First time babysitting?"

"Is it that obvious?" Isabella asked.

"You walked past my plot four times with your shoulders up around your ears," he said, and went back to his tomatoes, smiling.

The baby slept, buoyant and boneless in her swaddle, her small chest rising and falling. Tony came over with a crust still in his hand. "You should get a shirt that says ambassador of quiet babies," he said.

Isabella laughed, wiped her eyes with her wrist, and pushed the stroller into the shade. "Two more hours," she said. "I can do two more hours."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
story:
Eli kept the folded newspaper page in his pocket all morning, running his thumb over the crease. On it was a photo of the sign outside Hendricks Pharmacy: NO BACKPACKS, NO EXCEPTIONS. Two weeks ago a guard had stopped him at the door and made him carry his bag over his head like a criminal while Juliana watched. He had a civics assignment due tomorrow: explain one right from the Canadian Charter in his own words, in front of the whole class. He knew exactly which one he wanted, if he could prove he was right.

The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old paper. Mr. Torres led them down a marble hallway to Courtroom Four, where a lawyer in a grey suit was arguing a case about a city bylaw. Eli barely listened. He was waiting for the break, when the judge would leave and the lawyer might talk to them. "You get five minutes," Mr. Torres said, "so make your questions count."

The moment the session paused, Eli's hand went up before Juliana's, before Heinrich's. "A store by my house banned backpacks," he said, his voice louder than he meant. "That's against the Charter, right? Section fifteen says no discrimination, and it's biased against students, because we're the ones carrying backpacks."

The lawyer tilted her head. "Interesting question. Can you distinguish between a law and a store rule?"

"Sort of?" Eli said. "A law comes from the government."

"Right. And the Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals." She glanced at her watch, then back at him. "So think about who made the rule you're angry about."

Eli felt his ears go hot. A store wasn't the government. The Charter couldn't touch it, not directly, which meant his whole assignment was built on sand. He sat down hard beside Juliana.

"Your face," she whispered.

"I was wrong," he whispered back. "In front of everybody."

"So fix it. Section eight. Search and seizure. The police are the government, so the Charter actually applies there." She tapped his notebook. "Use your backpack thing anyway. Say the guard could search you and no Charter right would stop it, but a police officer couldn't just search you on the street."

Eli sat up. There was a kind of symmetry to it: the same bag, two different people holding it, two different sets of rules. He began writing fast, crossing out his first paragraph, drafting a second. Heinrich leaned over and pointed at a line, and Eli nodded and changed the word "unfair" to "no Charter protection."

When the lawyer gathered her files to leave, she paused at their row. "What did you decide?" she asked.

Eli stood. "The Charter is a leash on governments," he said. "It doesn't reach private stores. Not directly."

"That," she said, "is an explanation in your own words." She swung her bag over her shoulder and walked out through the tall doors.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
The last Saturday of September, the farmers' market smelled like cider and fried dough, and Theodore had eleven dollars and one plan: strawberries. Alvin had told him the berry table sold out by ten, so Theodore arrived at nine, Michael trailing behind with a granola bar he refused to share. The strawberry line already curled past the honey stand, and when Theodore reached the front, the price card read nine dollars a basket instead of the six he remembered from August.

"Nine?" he said. "They were six."

The vendor shrugged, not unkindly. "Frost took half the crop upstate this week. Everybody wants what's left."

Behind them, a man bought three baskets without blinking. The rows of berries gleamed red under the tent, and only eleven baskets sat on the table. Theodore paid nine dollars for one, and his pocket felt considerably lighter.

They wandered toward the cider press, where a woman in a linen apron was pressing apples with a long wooden crank, the juice hissing into a bucket. Beside her, on black velvet, a jeweler's case held a single diamond the size of a pea, priced at two thousand dollars. Michael leaned over it. "Why would that tiny rock cost more than a hundred bottles of cider?"

The jeweler, sorting receipts, said offhandedly, "Adam Smith asked something like that in 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776. Nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything. A diamond can buy a great deal."

Theodore stood very still, holding his strawberry basket. He looked at the cider, at the water bottles in the cooler selling for a dollar, at the pea-sized stone worth more than his bike, his backpack and his summer savings combined. Useful did not seem to be the point. There were lakes of water and only a handful of diamonds in the world, he supposed, and there had been mountains of strawberries in August and eleven baskets now.

He decided to test it. At the peach table, where crates were stacked to the awning and the seller looked almost desperate, he asked the price. Three dollars, down from four last month. He bought two, and the seller threw in a third for free, actually saying "please take them" with his eyes.

"Notice anything?" Theodore said, walking back with peaches tumbling against his strawberries.

"Inflation," Michael said, chewing a peach. "My dad says that word at breakfast."

"That's not it, though." Theodore frowned. "The berries cost more because there weren't many and everyone wanted them. The peaches cost less because there were too many. The water costs almost nothing and the diamond costs a fortune. It's like there's a rule underneath everything, and the prices are just the rule's shadow."

Alvin, who had spent his money on kettle corn, said, "You should sell that theory."

They passed Ms. Kelly from school, examining a pumpkin as if it owed her money. Theodore held up his peaches and said, "Want one? I got them cheap. Too many peaches this year."

She took one, and the diamond sparkled in its case across the aisle, and the strawberry vendor's table was empty by ten, just as Alvin had promised.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
story:
Sophia had chosen the cemetery because it was the quietest place within walking distance of her house, and quiet was what she needed. In three days she would stand in the gurdwara with her cousin and take her turn at the Khalsa initiation ceremony, and she still stumbled halfway through Japji Sahib, the long morning prayer she was supposed to know by heart. She sat on a flat stone near the fence, the photocopied pages trembling in the wind, and began again from the beginning.

Her eyes kept streaming, though not from frustration. The freshly cut grass had set off her pollen allergy, and every few lines she had to wipe her face on her sleeve and find her place again. She wondered whether the people who memorized these words centuries ago had also had to fight through wind and itchy eyes, or whether they had sat somewhere still and sealed, like a library.

Nolan found her there after twenty minutes, because he always cut through the cemetery on his way home from the coin shop. He flopped onto the grass beside her, careful of the headstones, and asked what the pages were. "A prayer I have to know by Sunday," Sophia said. "It's part of the ceremony." Nolan squinted at the script, which he could not read at all. "What's the ceremony called?" he asked. "Amrit Sanchar," she said. "My cousin went through it last spring. She had to know this prayer too, the whole thing, no paper."

While she recited, Nolan sorted through the change in his pocket, and after a while he held up a quarter with a dull edge. "This one's counterfeit," he said, turning it in the light. "Weight's wrong. My granddad showed me." Sophia looked at it, then at her pages, and an uncomfortable thought pressed on her. If she recited the words but didn't really know them, only patched them together from the paper, would that be a kind of counterfeit too? She tested the idea against herself, closing her eyes and trying the middle section without looking. She got six lines in before the words slid apart like wet sand.

So she tried something new. Instead of pushing straight through, she started saying the lines to the graves, slow and out loud, as if telling them to someone, because she had noticed she never forgot things she said to a person the way she forgot things she said to nobody. It was the same reason she could remember every word of an argument with her mother but not a single date from history class. Line by line, the words stopped being marks on a page and started being something she was handing over.

The wind opposed her, flipping the pages whenever it gusted, so she weighted them with Nolan's counterfeit quarter, which he said could at least be honest about something now. Ms. Sandhu, the neighbour who walked her dog along the fence every evening, slowed down to listen, and though Sophia faltered twice, she finished the whole prayer out loud without the paper.

On Sunday morning, in the bright hall with her cousin's hand steady on her shoulder, Sophia closed her eyes and began, and the words came the way they had come to the graves, unhurried and sure. When she reached the line where she always used to slip, she heard Nolan's voice in her memory saying, "Weight's wrong," and she sailed past it, smiling.
